clinicalPearls: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is an acquired clonal disorder caused by a somatic PIGA mutation in a haematopoietic stem cell, leading to loss of the GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55 and CD59.
Absence of CD55 and CD59 leaves red cells exposed to unregulated complement, producing chronic intravascular Coombs-negative haemolysis with haemoglobinuria.
The classic triad is intravascular haemolysis, a marked thrombotic tendency and a degree of bone marrow failure.
Thrombosis, often at unusual sites such as the hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal or cerebral veins, is the leading cause of death.
Smooth-muscle dystonia from nitric oxide scavenging by free haemoglobin causes abdominal pain, dysphagia, erectile dysfunction and fatigue disproportionate to anaemia.
There is a close relationship with aplastic anaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, and a PNH clone may emerge in that setting.
Diagnosis rests on flow cytometry demonstrating GPI-anchor-deficient cells, using fluorescent aerolysin (FLAER) and antibodies to GPI-linked proteins.
Terminal complement blockade markedly reduces haemolysis and thrombotic risk but mandates meningococcal vaccination beforehand because of the resulting terminal-pathway deficiency.
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria results from a somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a haematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor. Blood cells derived from this clone lack all GPI-anchored surface proteins, including the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis). Without these regulators, red cells cannot restrain the alternative pathway or the membrane attack complex on their surface, so complement lyses them, producing chronic intravascular haemolysis that worsens during complement-activating stresses such as infection. Liberated free haemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, causing smooth-muscle dystonia and promoting platelet activation, which, together with complement-mediated effects, underlies the characteristic thrombophilia. Clonal expansion is often favoured in the context of immune-mediated marrow failure.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of intravascular haemolysis including microangiopathy
Inherited or acquired thrombophilia with venous thrombosis
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood flow cytometry with FLAER and GPI-linked marker antibodies on multiple lineages
Markers of intravascular haemolysis: lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, reticulocytes and bilirubin
Full blood count and bone marrow examination to assess for marrow failure or myelodysplasia
Cross-sectional or Doppler imaging where thrombosis is suspected
Iron studies, as chronic urinary iron loss can cause deficiency
redFlags: New or worsening abdominal pain suggesting hepatic or mesenteric vein thrombosis
Neurological deficit or headache suggesting cerebral venous thrombosis
Breathlessness or hypoxia suggesting pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension
Rapidly falling blood counts indicating evolving marrow failure
Fever in a patient on terminal complement blockade, given meningococcal risk
reference.prognosis: The natural history is variable and can span many years, but thrombosis and progressive marrow failure are the principal causes of death; terminal complement inhibition has substantially improved survival and quality of life, and allogeneic stem cell transplantation remains the only curative option in selected cases.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because the direct antiglobulin test is negative, when Coombs-negativity is expected.
Overlooking paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria in unexplained venous thrombosis at unusual sites.
Failing to screen for a PNH clone in aplastic anaemia or myelodysplastic syndrome.
Starting terminal complement blockade without prior meningococcal vaccination and counselling.
Attributing fatigue and smooth-muscle symptoms solely to the degree of anaemia rather than to nitric oxide depletion.
references: International consensus guidelines on the diagnosis and management of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
management: Institute terminal complement blockade with an anti-C5 agent such as eculizumab or ravulizumab to control intravascular haemolysis and reduce thrombosis
Add a proximal complement inhibitor such as pegcetacoplan where clinically significant C3-mediated extravascular haemolysis persists despite C5 blockade
Immunise against meningococcus and other encapsulated organisms before complement inhibition, with prophylactic antibiotics to mitigate infection risk
Anticoagulate for thrombosis at typical or atypical venous sites, which remains the leading cause of death
Give supportive folic acid, iron replacement for urinary iron loss, and transfusion, and treat coexisting aplastic anaemia with immunosuppression such as antithymocyte globulin and ciclosporin
Monitor lactate dehydrogenase, reticulocytes, full blood count, and clone size by flow cytometry, with imaging surveillance for suspected thrombosis
Consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only curative treatment, for severe or transfusion-dependent marrow failure
Coordinate care through a specialist haematology centre
